h1: How Should a Breast Pump Flange Fit?
keywords: how should a breast pump flange fit
how should a flange fit on nipple
how should flange fit on breast
how should a flange fit when pumping
answer: A breast pump flange fits when your nipple sits centered in the tunnel and moves freely in and out without rubbing the sides, little or no areola is pulled in, and pumping feels comfortable. A common starting point is a tunnel a few millimeters wider than the base of your nipple.
intro: The flange (also called a breast shield) is the funnel-shaped piece that sits on the breast, and the size printed on it is the inside diameter of the tunnel in millimeters. Many pumps come with one or two sizes, often around 24 mm and 27 or 28 mm, but plenty of people need something smaller or larger. Nipple size can also differ between sides and change over the weeks of feeding, so it's worth checking fit more than once.

checklist.good: The nipple sits in the center of the tunnel and moves straight in and out with each pull.
checklist.tooTight: The nipple rubs or drags against the tunnel wall on one or more sides.
checklist.tooLoose: The nipple sways from side to side or drifts off-center during pumping.

checklist.good: A small, even gap around the nipple, roughly 1–2 mm on each side, as it moves.
checklist.tooTight: No visible gap: the nipple fills the tunnel and is squeezed as it's drawn in.
checklist.tooLoose: A wide gap, with the nipple swelling or stretching to fill a tunnel that's much bigger than it.

checklist.good: Little or none of the areola is pulled into the tunnel.
checklist.tooTight: The edge of the tunnel presses a ring into the areola at the base of the nipple.
checklist.tooLoose: A large part of the areola is drawn into the tunnel with each pull.

checklist.good: The flange rests flat with gentle contact all round and keeps suction without you pressing hard.
checklist.tooTight: You need to push the flange firmly into the breast to keep it sealed, which can block flow.
checklist.tooLoose: Suction keeps breaking, or air leaks at the edge even when the flange is centered.

checklist.good: The nipple looks much as it did before, perhaps slightly longer for a short time, with no marks.
checklist.tooTight: A white or red ring at the base, pinched or flattened edges, or a pale tip.
checklist.tooLoose: The nipple and areola look puffy or swollen, or are red and irritated around the base.

checklist.good: You feel tugging and pressure, but no pain, at a suction level that's comfortable for you.
checklist.tooTight: Pinching or rubbing, often worst at the base of the nipple.
checklist.tooLoose: A dragging or pulling feeling on the areola, sometimes with soreness after the session.

variations.heading: Fit by pump type and flange style
variations.intro: The same nipple-in-the-tunnel test applies to every pump. What differs is how the size is labeled and how adjustable it is.

items.name: Standard rigid flanges
items.text: Hard plastic funnels that come with most electric and manual pumps. They're sold in a range of sizes, but not every brand makes every size, and a flange from one brand usually only fits that brand's pump.

items.name: Flange inserts
items.text: Soft or rigid sleeves that sit inside a larger flange to make the tunnel smaller. They're a common way to get sizes below what a pump includes. Check the insert's labeled size, not the flange it sits in.

items.name: Soft or silicone flanges
items.text: These flex and can feel gentler, but softer material can collapse inward under suction and act smaller than its label. Judge the fit by watching the nipple, not just the number.

items.name: Wearable and in-bra pumps
items.text: The flange is built into a cup that sits inside the bra. Sizing works the same way, but the nipple can be harder to see, so many brands suggest checking alignment through the clear part of the cup. Their size labels may not line up exactly with standard flanges.

items.name: Hand pumps
items.text: The same sizing rules apply. Because you control the suction directly, a poor fit can be easy to miss; watch for rubbing and areola being pulled in.

measure.heading: How to measure your nipple for a flange
measure.intro: You're measuring the diameter of the nipple itself at its base, not the areola. A ruler with millimeter markings, a printable nipple ruler, or a sizing tool from a pump brand all work.
steps: Measure before pumping, or a little while after, when the nipple is in its usual resting state. Some people find gently rolling the nipple first gives a more consistent reading.
Hold the ruler or sizing tool across the base of the nipple where it meets the areola.
Read the width straight across in millimeters. Don't include any of the areola.
Repeat on the other side. It's common for the two sides to differ.
Add a few millimeters to find a starting flange size. A common rule is a tunnel about 2–4 mm larger than the nipple, so an 18 mm nipple would start around 20–22 mm.
Try that size while pumping and check it against the fit checklist. Adjust up or down based on what you see and feel.
Re-measure every few weeks, or whenever pumping becomes uncomfortable.
measure.tip: The few-millimeters rule is a starting point, not a guarantee. Brands measure and label flanges slightly differently, so the best fit is the one that passes the checklist.

problems.problem: Nipple rubs the tunnel or has a ring at the base
problems.fix: The flange is likely too small. Try the next size up, and re-measure the nipple at its base.

problems.problem: A lot of areola is pulled into the tunnel
problems.fix: The flange is likely too large. Try a smaller flange or an insert that reduces the tunnel size.

problems.problem: Pumping hurts even with the right size
problems.fix: Lower the suction to the highest level that's still comfortable, and check that the nipple is centered. Pain that continues, or any damage to the nipple, is worth discussing with a lactation consultant or doctor.

problems.problem: One side fits and the other doesn't
problems.fix: Use a different flange size on each side. Mixing sizes is common and fine as long as both fit the pump.

problems.problem: The size that fit at first doesn't fit now
problems.fix: Nipple size can change over time. Re-measure and try a different size rather than assuming the original is still right.

extra.heading: Why brands differ
extra.body: Flange sizes describe the tunnel's inside diameter, but brands vary in tunnel length, the angle of the funnel and the material. Two flanges with the same number can feel different. Some brands publish their own sizing guide or ruler with a recommended allowance, so it's worth checking the guidance for your pump. A lactation consultant can watch a pumping session and help you choose.

extra.heading: Getting help with sizing
extra.body: International Board Certified Lactation Consultants (IBCLCs), hospital lactation services and some pump suppliers offer flange fitting. It helps to bring your pump and the flanges you've tried. Ask your insurer or pump supplier whether replacement flanges or inserts in other sizes are covered.

picks.label: Flange inserts in smaller sizes
picks.why: A low-cost way to try sizes below what your pump includes, using the flanges you already have.

picks.label: Replacement flanges in your pump's brand
picks.why: Lets you try the next size up or down; check that it's made for your specific pump model.

picks.label: Nipple ruler or flange sizing tool
picks.why: Makes it easier to measure the nipple base in millimeters than with a standard ruler.

picks.label: Soft silicone flange cushions
picks.why: Some people find them more comfortable. Watch that they don't make the tunnel act smaller than labeled.

faqs.q: How should a flange fit on the nipple?
faqs.a: The nipple should be centered in the tunnel and move freely in and out without rubbing the sides, with a small gap all round and little or no areola pulled in.

faqs.q: How should a flange fit on the breast?
faqs.a: It should rest flat against the breast with gentle contact all round, keeping suction without you having to press it in hard. Pressing too firmly can restrict milk flow.

faqs.q: How do I know if my flange is too small?
faqs.a: The nipple rubs or drags on the tunnel walls, pumping pinches, or you see a white or red ring at the base of the nipple afterward.

faqs.q: How do I know if my flange is too big?
faqs.a: Much of the areola is pulled into the tunnel, the nipple swings from side to side, or the nipple and areola look swollen after pumping.

faqs.q: How much bigger than my nipple should the flange be?
faqs.a: A common rule is a few millimeters, often about 2–4 mm larger than the nipple diameter at its base. Treat that as a starting point and adjust based on how it looks and feels.

faqs.q: Can I use different flange sizes on each side?
faqs.a: Yes. Nipples often differ in size, and using a different flange on each side is common.

faqs.q: How should a flange fit when pumping compared with before?
faqs.a: The nipple naturally lengthens and moves in the tunnel while pumping. The fit is right if it still moves freely without rubbing and doesn't fill the tunnel or pull in the areola.

caution: This page covers general flange fit only. Pain, nipple damage, signs of infection or concerns about milk supply should be discussed with a lactation consultant (IBCLC) or your doctor.
